We declared so loudly and earnestly that we were free men that we caught the attention of that liberty-spouting speaker and his patriotic audience. They gathered around us, looking very determined. The speaker said:

“If you really are free men, you have nothing to fear. Britain’s God-given liberties surround you as your shield and shelter! (Applause.) You will soon see. Present your evidence.”

“What evidence?”

“Evidence that you are free men.”

Ah—I remembered! My senses returned, and I said nothing. But the king burst out:

“You’re mad, man. It would be better, and much more reasonable, to make this thief and scoundrel prove that we are not free men.”

You see, he knew his own laws as people so often know laws: as words, without knowing their effects. They acquire meaning, and become remarkably vivid, when they are applied to you.

Everyone shook their heads in disappointment; some lost interest and turned away. The speaker continued, this time with businesslike tones instead of emotion:

“If you don’t know your country’s laws, it is time you learned them. You are strangers here; you cannot deny that. You may be free men; we do not deny that. But you may also be slaves. The law is clear: the claimant need not prove you are slaves. You must prove you are not.”

I said:

“Dear sir, just give us time to send to Astolat, or to the Valley of Holiness—”

“Quiet, my good man. These are extraordinary requests, and you cannot expect them to be granted. They would take considerable time and impose an unjustified inconvenience on your master—”

“Master, you idiot!” the king roared. “I have no master. I myself am the m—”

“Be quiet, for God’s sake!”

I spoke just in time to stop him. We were already in enough trouble; letting these people think we were lunatics would hardly improve matters.

There is no point drawing out the details. The earl offered us for sale and auctioned us off. This very same hellish law had existed in our own South in my own time, more than thirteen hundred years later. Under it, hundreds of free men unable to prove their freedom had been sold into lifelong slavery without making much impression on me. But the moment the law and the auction block touched my own life, what had merely seemed improper suddenly became monstrous. Well, that is how we are made.

Yes, we were auctioned like pigs. In a large town with a busy market we would have fetched a good price. But this place was utterly stagnant, and we sold for a sum that still embarrasses me whenever I remember it.

I regard it as among the earliest refinements of cultivated society.”

“Certainly, sir; and it enjoys the further advantage of being fashionable among the world’s less cultivated societies as well. Every savage knows how to dance.”

Sir William merely smiled. “Your friend dances charmingly,” he went on after a pause, noticing Bingley approach the group; “and I am sure you yourself are accomplished in the art, Mr. Darcy.”

“I believe you watched me dance at Meryton, sir.”

“Indeed I did, and the sight gave me considerable pleasure. Do you dance frequently at St. James’s?”

“Never, sir.”

“Would you not consider it a fitting compliment to the place?”

“It is a compliment I pay no place when I can help it.”

“You have a house in London, I suppose?”

Mr. Darcy inclined his head.

“I once considered settling in town myself, for I enjoy superior company; but I was not entirely satisfied that London’s air would suit Lady Lucas.”

He stopped, expecting a reply, but his companion showed no inclination to offer one. Elizabeth happened just then to be approaching, and the idea of performing a particularly gallant act struck him. He called to her:

“My dear Miss Eliza, why are you not dancing? Mr. Darcy, you must permit me to recommend this young lady as a most desirable partner. Surely you cannot decline a dance with such beauty standing before you.” Taking her hand, he was about to place it in Mr. Darcy’s. Though greatly surprised, Darcy was willing enough to accept it; but she immediately withdrew, saying to Sir William with some agitation:

“Truly, sir, I have no intention whatever of dancing. Pray do not imagine that I came this way to solicit a partner.”

With solemn courtesy Mr. Darcy asked for the honour of her hand, but to no purpose. Elizabeth remained firm, and Sir William’s efforts to persuade her did nothing to alter her decision.

“You dance so excellently, Miss Eliza, that it is cruel to deprive me of the pleasure of watching you. Though this gentleman generally dislikes the diversion, I am certain he cannot object to obliging us for half an hour.”

“Mr. Darcy is politeness itself,” Elizabeth said, smiling.

“He certainly is; yet with such an inducement, my dear Miss Eliza, his willingness can hardly surprise us. Who could object to a partner like you?”

Elizabeth gave an arch look and turned away. Her refusal had not diminished her standing with the gentleman. He was thinking of her with some satisfaction when Miss Bingley addressed him as follows:

The storm continued furiously throughout the night, yet nothing especially remarkable happened. When the family came downstairs to breakfast the next morning, however, the dreadful bloodstain lay on the floor once more. “I cannot think the Paragon Detergent is to blame,” Washington said, “because I have tested it on everything. It must be the ghost.” He therefore removed the stain again, but on the second morning it returned. It was present on the third morning too, although Mr. Otis had personally locked the library overnight and taken the key upstairs. By now the entire family was thoroughly interested. Mr. Otis suspected he had denied the existence of ghosts too positively; Mrs. Otis announced her intention to enter the Psychical Society; and Washington composed a lengthy letter to Messrs. Myers and Podmore concerning the Permanence of Sanguineous Stains in Connection with Crime. That night every doubt about the objective existence of phantoms was dispelled forever.

The day had been sunny and warm, and the family all went driving in the evening’s coolness. They arrived home only at nine, and ate a light supper. Their talk never turned toward ghosts, so even the preliminary state of expectant receptivity that so often precedes psychic manifestations was absent. As I afterward learned from Mr. Otis, they discussed only the usual topics of cultivated Americans of the better class: Miss Fanny Davenport’s immense superiority to Sarah Bernhardt as an actress; the difficulty of finding green corn, buckwheat cakes, or hominy even in the finest English households; Boston’s importance to the development of the world-soul; the merits of the baggage-check system for railway journeys; and the sweetness of a New York accent beside the London drawl. The supernatural went entirely unmentioned, and there was no reference whatever to Sir Simon de Canterville. At eleven the family went to bed, and by half past eleven every light was extinguished. Some time later, a peculiar sound in the passage outside his bedroom woke Mr. Otis. It resembled the clanking of metal and appeared to draw closer by the moment. He rose immediately, struck a match, and checked the time: precisely one o’clock. Perfectly composed, he felt his pulse and found no trace of fever. The curious noise persisted, now accompanied by clearly audible footsteps. Slipping on his slippers, he removed a small oblong bottle from his dressing case and opened the door.
